O.outcome_detail: coverage and concentration of the 14 learning objectives

cells.quote: The FCI [1] is a 30-item multiple-choice assessment that probes students’ conceptual understanding of force and motion, contrasting Newtonian reasoning with common informal beliefs about mechanics. Physics instructors use it more widely than any other mechanics RBA [4]. The FMCE [2] covers content similar to the FCI, kinematics and Newton’s laws, in 47 multiple-choice items. Several items share a physical scenario and ask students to select the response consistent with their reasoning about that scenario. The FMCE includes a small number of items on energy. The EMCS [3] is a 25-item multiple-choice assessment focused on energy and momentum, covering concepts such as kinetic and potential energy, work, and conservation principles that the FCI and FMCE do not address. Together, these three assessments cover the core topics of introductory mechanics.
cells.note: The entry additionally reports that the three RBAs cover all 14 LOs with at least six items per LO; that exact coverage result is not stated in the supplied study text excerpt.

O.outcome_detail: adoption of RBIS in additional courses

cells.quote: Twenty-three of the 25 RBIS users on the PHAS faculty were found to be using RBIS in additional courses. Four of the 29 non-quitting EOAS faculty have not taught a different undergraduate course. Of the remaining 25, 23 have implemented RBIS in additional courses.
cells.note: This is a descriptive follow-up among faculty who had adopted RBIS with CWSEI support; the comparison is between those who did and did not subsequently use RBIS in another course, not a randomized treatment comparison.

D.comparison: earlier period before or during less CWSEI involvement

O.outcome_detail: faculty belief in research-based instructional strategies

cells.quote: There were some other faculty members in every department who did not believe in RBIS and simply refused to use them. The fraction of the faculty with those beliefs has noticeably decreased over time in every department that has a CWSEI supported initiative. In EOAS, where there has been the most widespread involvement, with about ¾ of the faculty having worked with an SES, it is now nearly zero, and in PHAS it has dropped markedly with time, although it still remains a significant fraction.
cells.note: The authors describe this as an impression based on their work with faculty; the text states that they do not have data on the fraction in some other departments.
